props.title: Simple Plan

sections.content: Sam Raimi's Simple Plan (1998) marks a masterful shift from his horror roots into stark moral thriller territory. Like Fargo (1996), it explores how ordinary people spiral into darkness after discovering criminal money. Bill Paxton and Billy Bob Thornton deliver career-best performances as brothers whose lives unravel after finding $4.4 million in crashed plane. The snow-covered Minnesota setting becomes a character itself, with cinematographer Alar Kivilo capturing the bleakness that mirrors the characters' moral decay. The film shares DNA with A History of Violence (2005) and No Country for Old Men (2007) in examining how quick decisions lead to inescapable consequences.

sections.content: The film represents a crucial moment in 90s neo-noir, alongside Red Rock West (1993) and The Last Seduction (1994). What sets Simple Plan apart is its intimate focus on family bonds and small-town dynamics. The relationship between the brothers - one educated and respected, the other simple but genuine - creates devastating moral complexity. Scott B. Smith adapted his own novel, maintaining the book's crushing sense of inevitability while adding visual poetry to the moral decay. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Rural Noir

Simple Plan helped establish a vital subgenre of rural crime films that continued with Winter's Bone (2010) and Hell or High Water (2016). These films share an emphasis on economic desperation in forgotten American communities, where crime becomes a twisted form of survival. The film's influence can be seen in recent works like Wind River (2017), where the isolation of snow-covered landscapes amplifies moral choices and their consequences.
